definition.text: Buying and selling water access entitlements, often called water rights, between willing sellers and buyers.

facts.text: A seller holds water rights beyond its current needs, while a buyer short of water is willing to pay for more.
Economic theory says trading moves water from less to more economically productive uses; urban users can pay up to 10 times more than farmers.
First-in-time prior appropriation rights led to inefficient allocation and less adoption of water-saving technology.
Water is a common-pool resource that behaves like a private good once rights make its use rival and excludable.
Trades can harm or help third parties who are neither buyer nor seller.
Water is not a standard commodity: supply is uncertain and moves through complex systems, and supply swings can leave markets thin.
Schemes exist in the western United States, Chile, South Africa, Australia and elsewhere; some consider Australia's the most sophisticated.
Chile's 1981 Water Code made water rights freely tradable private property, a strongly free-market approach that has been controversial.

definition.text: A border carbon adjustment: a tariff on the carbon embedded in imported goods, usually to stop carbon leakage from places without a carbon price.

facts.text: Likely targets include electricity from coal-fired power stations, iron and steel from blast furnaces, and fertilizer from the Haber process.
California has applied one to imported electricity since 2011, and the EU and UK apply them from 2026 and 2027.
Border adjustment is considered an economically efficient fix for leakage, but it might disguise trade protectionism.
Current WTO rules may prohibit some types, and the WTO has not reached a conclusion.
Adjusting imports but not exports reduces the global competitiveness of domestic carbon-intensive products.

definition.text: A tradable Kyoto Protocol unit allowing a country to emit one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent.

facts.text: Units were issued up to each Annex 1 country's Kyoto emission target for the 2008–2012 commitment period.
Under Article 17, countries below their targets could sell spare units to countries above theirs.
Such trading had to be supplemental to domestic action.

title: CORSIA
article: Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation

definition.text: The Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, which makes airlines buy carbon credits to offset growth in emissions from international flights.

facts.text: The International Civil Aviation Organization adopted it in October 2016, aiming for carbon-neutral growth from 2020.
It is voluntary from 2021 until 2027, when it becomes compulsory; least developed and small island states are not required to join.
Domestic flights are not included, and it will regulate 25% of aviation's international emissions.
Critics say it won't reduce jet fuel demand, and one hundred organisations rejected it as letting warming pass 1.5 °C.

contested_note: Supporters call it a compromise step forward, while environmental groups argue it will not cut aviation emissions enough.

definition.text: Permanently removing emission allowances or carbon credits from circulation so they can never be sold or used again.

facts.text: Retiring allowances shrinks supply under a cap, which raises their scarcity and price.
The EU's Market Stability Reserve invalidated about 2.5 billion allowances on 1 January 2023, and more than 3 billion by 2026.
In voluntary markets, companies retire credits to offset emissions they cannot yet eliminate; a record 164 million were retired in 2023.
Citizen groups have bought and retired sulfur dioxide allowances in US EPA auctions to cut the supply available to polluters.

definition.text: A carbon credit issued by the Clean Development Mechanism for verified emission cuts made by its projects under the Kyoto Protocol.

facts.text: Each unit equals a cut of one tonne of CO2e, measured against a baseline.
Annex I countries buy them from projects in developing countries, where cuts are cheapest, and can use them to meet their targets.
Between 2001 and 7 September 2012 the CDM issued 1 billion CERs; by 2013, 57% came from destroying HFC-23 or N2O.
Prices fell from $20 a tonne in August 2008 to below $5 by September 2012 amid recession and EU ETS over-allocation.
